w: Stretching 511.5 metres into Gdansk Bay from the middle of Sopot's beach, this wooden pier has drawn promenaders since it opened in 1827, making it the longest wooden pier in Europe (Southend's is longer at 2,158 metres, but built of iron). At its tip, sea air reportedly carries twice the iodine found on land.
_facts: Opened 1827, 511.5m long, longest wooden pier in Europe
Iodine concentration at the tip said to be twice that on land
Southend Pier is longer overall (2,158m) but made of iron

w: Built in 1903-04 as part of Sopot's Balneological Institute, this lighthouse has since had its beam trimmed back to seven nautical miles - technically too short to count as a real lighthouse by modern standards, though everyone still calls it one. It remains open to visitors, a working landmark you can walk into.
s: A lighthouse built into a 1900s spa institute
_facts: Built 1903-04 as part of the Balneological Institute
Focal range reduced to 7 nautical miles, no longer technically a lighthouse

w: Facing Gdansk Bay from Sopot's beachfront, the Sofitel Grand Sopot operates as a historic five-star resort hotel, its facade protected as an architectural heritage monument. Alongside the pier next door, it anchors the stretch of seafront that built Sopot's identity as one of Poland's best-known coastal resorts.
s: A historic five-star beachfront hotel, Sopot's icon
_facts: Historic five-star beachfront resort hotel on Gdansk Bay
Registered as an architectural heritage monument
